There is no lead in your pencil.
In four minutes, a tree and a rock become this pencil.
On the way, they pass through an oven at about eleven hundred degrees.
And it all hangs on a glued seam you've never noticed.
So why do we call it lead?
In the fifteen hundreds, a pure black rock turned up in Borrowdale, in northern England.
It was so pure, it could be sawn straight into sticks.
It looked like lead and marked like lead, so people called it black lead.
In seventeen seventy-nine, it turned out to be carbon.
Ten years later it was named graphite, from the Greek for to write.
Then war cut France off from English graphite.
So in seventeen ninety-five, Nicolas-Jacques Conté mixed powdered graphite with clay, and baked it.
Pencil cores are still made that way.
Zoom into that grey line, and something strange appears.
Graphite is carbon atoms, locked into flat sheets of hexagons.
In a sheet, each atom grips three neighbours tightly.
But the sheets are only loosely stacked.
Press down and drag, and the top sheets slide off, like cards from a deck.
Those loose flakes catch in the paper fibres. That's your line.
Here's the twist: a diamond is made of the same atoms.
Same carbon. One is the hardest mineral, the other one of the softest.
Pure graphite, though, is too soft to work on its own.
So the core starts as two powders: graphite and clay.
Add water, and they're ground together into a smooth grey paste.
The paste is squeezed through a tiny hole into long, thin strings.
The strings are cut to length and left to dry.
Then they go into a kiln, at about eleven hundred degrees Celsius.
The heat bakes the clay into hard cores.
A dip in hot wax fills the pores, so the core glides.
So why do some pencils write darker than others?
More graphite: a softer core, and a darker line.
More clay: a harder core, and a lighter line.
Most scales run from nine H, the hardest, to nine B, the softest.
H B is in the middle: in the US, the number two pencil.
Now, the wood. And the core still has to get inside it.
Many pencils are made from incense cedar.
The logs are cut into blocks, then into thin slats.
Each slat is about eighteen centimetres long, and just over half a centimetre thick.
The slats are dried, stained and waxed.
Then a cutter carves parallel grooves along each slat.
Each groove is only half as deep as a core.
Why half? Because every core gets two slats.
Glue goes on first. Then a core drops into every groove.
A second slat lands on top, and the stack goes into a press.
The press holds it until the glue sets.
So your pencil was never one piece.
That glue line runs the full length of every wooden pencil.
Cutters shape the sandwich into hexagons.
Six to nine pencils from every sandwich.
Two wooden halves glued around a core is an old idea. It's still how it's done.
But right now, these pencils are bare wood. They need colour.
Each pencil gets coat after coat of paint.
Layer by layer, a smooth, hard shell.
The eraser has its own story.
In eighteen fifty-eight, a Philadelphia stationer patented a pencil with an attached eraser.
Seventeen years later, the US Supreme Court declared that patent invalid.
Today, a metal ferrule is clamped on, and the eraser is pushed inside.
One last stamp marks the grade.
Two cedar halves. A baked core. One glue line. Paint, metal and rubber.
A tree and a rock, through the fire, and into your hand.
And every line it draws is graphite. Never lead.
